posts.title: What you should hand an AI agent
posts.excerpt: An agent is useful when it owns a bounded job, a small set of tools, and a person who reviews the exceptions.
posts.body:
Most agent projects start with a model and a long prompt. The ones that stay in production start with a job description.

Give the agent one outcome, the systems it may touch, and the cases it must hand back to a person. A support agent that can read an order, draft a reply, and open a ticket is easier to trust than an agent that is allowed to do anything in the inbox.

The review step is part of the product. Exceptions, refunds, and anything that changes money or access should land in a queue with the source material attached. That is how a team learns where the agent is confident and where the process is still unclear.

ATwebTech builds these as systems: the model, the tools, the logs, and the handoff. If the job cannot be explained in a few sentences, it is not ready to be automated.

posts.title: Chatbots stall after the demo
posts.excerpt: A polished demo answers the happy path. A working chatbot has to survive the questions your team did not script.
posts.body:
The demo conversation is usually the one everyone rehearsed. The real traffic is shorter, messier, and full of questions that belong to another department.

Before a chatbot goes on a site, write down the handful of jobs it is allowed to finish. Checking an order, booking a call, and explaining a plan are finishable. Open-ended advice about a contract is not, unless a person is on the other side of that path.

Keep the transcript, the source it used, and the point where it escalated. Those three records tell you what to teach next. Without them, every improvement is a guess.

The interface can be quiet. The work is in the boundaries: what the bot knows, when it should stop, and how a person picks the conversation up without asking the customer to start over.

posts.title: Automate the workflow you already trust
posts.excerpt: Start with the process your team can already explain. Automation should shorten that path, not invent a new one.
posts.body:
A workflow is ready for automation when someone can walk it from the first email to the last handoff. If the steps change depending on who is in the office, the model will copy that confusion.

Pick a process with a clear input and a clear done state. Intake, qualification, document collection, and status updates are common places to begin. The system should do the repetitive reading and routing, then leave a record a person can audit.

Measure the queue, not the model. Did the work move faster? Did fewer items come back? Did the team stop retyping the same details into a second tool?

That is the standard we use with clients. The technology can be ambitious. The first release should be a process the business already believes in.

services.title: Machine Learning
services.summary: Custom ML models trained on your proprietary data. Predictive, adaptive, and continuously improving as your business grows.
points: A model tied to a decision your team already makes
Training data you are allowed to use
A way to see when the model is unsure
A path to retrain when the business changes
services.body:
A model is worth building when it changes a decision you already make: which lead to call, which order looks wrong, which ticket should go first.

We use the records you already keep, and we say plainly when those records are too thin. The output is a score or a label a person can check, not a black box dropped into the business.

The work includes the first model, the place it shows up in the product, and the habit of looking at the misses. That is how it stays useful after the launch week.

services.title: Computer Vision
services.summary: Real-time image and video analysis — object detection, quality inspection, facial recognition, and automated visual reporting at scale.
points: Inspection, counting, and document capture
A human review step for anything that affects a person
Photos and video from the cameras or phones you already have
A report your operators can read without a data team
services.body:
Vision projects work when the camera is looking at a job a person can already describe. A scratch on a part, a missing label, a form that needs the fields pulled out.

We are careful with anything that identifies a person. If a use case needs that, it is scoped with the review and the retention rules up front, not added after the demo.

The result is a check on the line or in the upload flow, plus a record of what the system saw. Operators can override it. That override is how the next version gets better.

services.title: NLP Solutions
services.summary: Extract meaning, sentiment, and structured insights from unstructured text. Summarization, classification, translation — all unified.
points: Sort incoming mail, tickets, and reviews
Summaries that keep the source attached
Fields pulled out of contracts, forms, and notes
Language support for the customers you actually serve
services.body:
Most companies already have the text. It sits in inboxes, tickets, call notes, and reviews. The useful step is turning that pile into a queue someone can act on.

We classify, summarize, and pull out the fields your process needs. Every summary points back to the sentence it came from, so a person can check it before it changes a record.

For U.S. teams this often starts with support email or sales notes. Translation is added when you have a real second audience, not as a feature nobody asked to maintain.

services.title: AI Consulting
services.summary: Strategic AI roadmaps tailored to your industry. We audit your current stack, identify high-ROI opportunities, and guide implementation.
points: A look at the tools and the process, not just the model
A short list of jobs worth doing first
A build plan with owners and a review step
A recommendation to wait, when the data is not ready
services.body:
Consulting here is a decision about what to build, and what to leave alone. We sit with the people who do the work, map the path from the first request to the last handoff, and name the step that is slow for a boring reason.

The output is a short plan: the job, the systems it touches, the person who reviews exceptions, and the first release. If the records are too messy to support a model, we say so.

U.S. companies usually use this before a build, or when a pilot stalled after the demo. The point is a next step the team can start, not a slide about the future of AI.

services.title: Predictive Analytics
services.summary: Forecast customer behavior, supply chain demand, and market trends with precision models built on your historical and real-time data.
points: Forecasts tied to a decision, such as staffing or inventory
History you can actually trust
A plain explanation of what moved the number
A check against what happened last month
services.body:
A forecast is only useful if someone will do something different because of it. Order more, staff the afternoon, call the accounts that are about to go quiet.

We build that from the history you have: orders, seasons, pipeline, and the exceptions your team already knows about. The page shows the number and the few factors behind it, so a manager can disagree with the model using their own knowledge.

We do not promise a perfect read of the market. We build a forecast you can compare with what actually happened, and we adjust it when the business changes.
